answer.title: Energy takes gold's old job
answer.oneLine: Energy will not become the money you spend, but it is becoming the hard limit on what money can buy and the collateral behind new dollar loans.
answer.picture: Picture a party where the host hands out drink tickets. In the old days the number of tickets was capped by the drinks in the cellar, and that cellar was gold. In an AI and robot economy the cellar is the power plant: you can print more tickets, but you cannot print more electricity to pour. The tickets stay dollars, but the power supply sets how much they can really buy.
steps: Until 1971 gold was the scarce physical thing that capped how much real output any money could claim.
After 1971 the cap became political: how much debt the bond market would absorb.
In an AI and robot economy, output grows with delivered electric power, and power cannot be printed. So energy becomes the real ceiling.

Energy also enters as collateral inside the dollar. Power plants, data centers, power purchase agreements and GPUs back new dollar loans. The desk calls this the watt-dollar, heir to the 1974 petrodollar.
Energy fails as money you spend, because a kilowatt-hour is perishable, tied to a place, and keeps getting cheaper as solar scales.
Musk's idea of currency 'measured in power, wattage and tonnage' is a post-scarcity accounting unit. Its real problem is who sets the allocations.

terms.d: Something valuable you pledge to a lender. If you do not repay, the lender can take it.
The desk's name for dollar loans backed by energy assets such as power plants, data centers and GPUs. The loan is in dollars, the backing is energy.
The 1974 system where oil was priced in dollars and Gulf oil money was recycled into US Treasury bonds.
A unit of electricity: the energy a 1,000-watt device uses in one hour. It is what your power bill counts.
A long contract to buy electricity from a power plant at a set price. Lenders treat it as a reliable future income.
A hoped-for future where robots and cheap energy make most goods so plentiful that normal prices stop mattering.

answer.why: Your pay will stay in dollars through at least 2030. But the price of electricity is becoming a hidden driver of what those dollars buy. PJM wholesale power rose 41% in 2026, and rising power prices near data centers erode fixed incomes.

connects.how: The map shows how this answer could play out from today through 2050, including the small energy standard branch.
The watt-dollar lives inside the dollar system that the board section describes.
China's controls on magnets, batteries and solar parts aim straight at the watt-dollar.

check.q: Why would a coin pegged to one kilowatt-hour lose value over time?
check.a: Because electricity keeps getting cheaper as solar scales, so one kWh buys less over time. It is also perishable and tied to a place, which is why every energy currency since Henry Ford's 1921 proposal failed.

future.title: A map of possible money futures
future.oneLine: Starting from today's dollar system, the world could drift toward one of four money systems, and the odds of each shift as time passes.
future.picture: Picture a river leaving a lake and splitting into four channels downstream. Today the widest channel is the dollar extension. As you float further, to 2035 and then 2050, some channels widen and others narrow, but none is guaranteed. On the map, the thickness of each band is how likely that channel is.
steps: Start at today: the dollar dominates, and stablecoins are still small (4.3% of T-bills).
H0, now to 2028: S1 dollar extension 62%, S4 disorderly reset 22%, S2 neutral layer 15%, S3 energy standard 1%.
H1, 2028 to 2035: S1 falls to 45%, S4 rises to 30%, S2 grows to 22%, S3 reaches 3%.
H2, 2035 to 2050: S1 32%, S4 30%, S2 28%, S3 10%. No single path is above one in three.
The scenarios can coexist. S2 growing does not mean S1 fails.

terms.d: A time window. H0 is now to 2028, H1 is 2028 to 2035, H2 is 2035 to 2050.
Stablecoins and tokenized Treasuries carry the dollar onto new digital rails. The dollar stays in charge.
Gold, and possibly Bitcoin, settle payments between nations, while people still use dollars every day.
A unit based on physics, such as energy or computing power, used for machine-to-machine commerce.
Heavy debt forces high inflation, caps on interest rates or a crisis first, and a new system is built afterward.
How likely something is, from 0 (never) to 100 (certain). Here each horizon's four numbers add up to 100.

future.why: These odds tell you how much weight to give 'the dollar is ending' headlines. Even by 2050 the dollar-led path is still the single most likely one, but the chance of a messy reset is about three in ten. Knowing that helps you tell fear-selling from evidence.

connects.how: The scenarios table holds the same numbers that set the band widths on this map.
The tripwires are the signals that would make one band grow or shrink.
The energy answer explains why the S3 band stays thin even by 2050.

check.q: In H2 (2035 to 2050), which scenario is still the most likely, and at what odds?
check.a: S1 dollar extension at 32%, just ahead of S4 disorderly reset at 30% and S2 neutral layer at 28%.

debt.title: Who buys the debt
debt.oneLine: The Fed and Treasury are not shrinking the $40.44T federal debt, they are arranging who must buy it.
debt.picture: Picture a treadmill. Its speed is the interest rate on the debt, and your running pace is how fast the economy grows. On top of that, each year someone tosses a new sandbag onto your back: the primary deficit. The government's plan is not to drop the sandbags but to line up helpers who are required to carry some of them.
steps: Gross federal debt is $40.44T. FY2026 net interest was $1,051.8B, above defense spending for a third year.
The average cost of the debt is 3.52%, but today's 10-year yield is 5.13%, and 70% of the debt reprices within 5 years.
The primary deficit, 2.9% of GDP, drives the debt ratio more than interest rates do.
The chosen route is captive demand. From 2027-01-18 stablecoin reserves must sit in short bills, banks get leverage relief, and Treasury buys back long bonds.
The passive route: nominal growth near 6% beats the 3.5% average debt cost, which quietly erodes the debt ratio.
Not chosen: revaluing gold (still booked at $42.22 an ounce) or buying Bitcoin.

terms.d: The gap between what the government spends and what it collects in taxes, not counting interest. It is new borrowing for current spending.
The interest the government pays on its debt, minus interest it earns. In FY2026 it was about $1.05 trillion.
A short-term IOU from the US government, lasting a year or less. It is seen as the safest dollar asset.
Buyers who are required by rules to hold government debt, such as stablecoin issuers under the new law.
Keeping interest rates below inflation so the real value of debt shrinks. Savers quietly pay for it.
The yearly return a bond pays, as a percent of its price. When yields rise, new borrowing costs more.

debt.why: Interest on the debt now costs more than the military. If an oil-driven inflation shock forced the Fed to cap yields, savers would quietly lose buying power. The desk names that as the path to the disorderly scenario.

connects.how: The weak spot in this plan is the road to S4, the disorderly reset.
Round 2 shows how stablecoins become required buyers of short Treasury bills.
Net interest at 19.5% of receipts, with a 25% tripwire, is the gauge to watch for this section.

check.q: Which drives the US debt ratio more: interest rates or the primary deficit?
check.a: The primary deficit. At 2.9% of GDP it matters more than the gap between the real rate and growth, which is only +0.26 points.

board.title: The new monopoly board
board.oneLine: Crypto and stablecoins are not merging with the old money system as equals, the old system is buying the new rails.
board.picture: Think of a big supermarket chain buying a trendy food truck. The truck keeps its paint and its app, but the ingredients now come from the chain's warehouse, and the chain keeps the profit. Stablecoins are the food truck, and short Treasury bills are the warehouse.
steps: Set 1 is gold, bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is crypto, stablecoins and AI payment rails.
The Federal Reserve stays the bank. Fedwire remains the place where payments become final.
By law, every compliant stablecoin dollar must be backed by short Treasury bills.
Issuers keep the interest on those bills. Holders get none, by law.
Physical gold sits in the neutral corner between nations. Bitcoin is a frozen government stockpile and ETF asset (1.29M BTC), not a reserve asset yet.
Rival boards: China chose a public e-CNY and banned stablecoins. The EU plans a digital euro around 2029.

terms.d: A digital token designed to stay worth exactly one dollar, backed by safe assets held by the company that issues it.
The moment a payment is truly final and the money has really changed hands.
The interest earned on money that customers park with a company. For stablecoins the issuer keeps it.
Central bank digital currency: digital cash issued directly by a central bank. US law bans one until 2030-12-31.
A normal bank deposit turned into a digital token that can move on a blockchain, still owed by the bank.

board.why: The money app on your phone may look new, but the same old assets sit behind it. Your crypto dollar is only as safe as the Treasury bills under it, and the interest on your idle balance goes to the issuer, not to you.

connects.how: Round 2 tests this acquisition story in detail: does Set 1 survive the new rails?
Stablecoins become required buyers of the bills that fund the debt.
The Round 2 summary, new rails on old anchors, grows directly from this board.

check.q: Under US law, who earns the interest on the Treasury bills that back a stablecoin?
check.a: The issuer and its distribution partners. The person holding the stablecoin gets none, by law.

scenarios.title: Four futures, with odds
scenarios.oneLine: The desk gives a probability to each of four possible money systems at the end of each time window, and each row adds up to 100.
scenarios.picture: Think of a weather forecast that says 62% chance of sun and 22% chance of storms. It does not promise sun. It tells you how to pack. These scenario odds work the same way for the money system.
steps: S1 dollar extension: stablecoins and tokenized Treasuries carry the dollar onto new rails.
S2 neutral reserve layer: gold and possibly Bitcoin settle between nations while the dollar stays for daily use.
S3 energy or compute standard: a physics-based unit for machine commerce.
S4 disorderly reset: debt forces inflation, yield caps or a crisis first, and a new system is built after.
Each row sums to 100. S1 falls from 62 (H0) to 32 (H2), while S4 rises from 22 to 30.
These are judgment calls, rated Speculative at 50, anchored to the evidence in the thesis cards.

terms.d: A possible version of the future, described clearly enough that you can tell later whether it happened.
When government debt is so large that the central bank has to help fund it instead of fighting inflation.
A central bank promise to buy bonds so that their interest rate cannot rise above a set level.
A US government bond represented as a digital token, so it can move and settle on a blockchain.
The measuring stick for prices. Today in the US that is the dollar.

scenarios.why: Odds help you avoid all-or-nothing thinking. A 22% chance of a messy reset before 2028 is not a prediction of collapse, but it is too high to ignore. Any plan built on just one story about money is fragile.

connects.how: The animated map draws these same odds as bands of different thickness.
The tripwires say which scenario is gaining ground.
Card Db-09 is where the debate court ruled on these probabilities.

check.q: If S2 (the neutral reserve layer) grows, does that mean S1 (dollar extension) has failed?
check.a: No. The scenarios can coexist. Gold could settle between nations while the dollar stays the money people use every day.

views.title: Three seats at the table
views.oneLine: The same money trends look different for a government, a business, and a person living on wages or a basic income.
views.picture: Picture three people in one house during a storm. The one fixing the roof (government) worries about leaks. The shopkeeper downstairs (business) worries about customers. The tenant (wage earner) worries about the heating bill. Same storm, three different worries.
steps: Governance: the real lever is the primary deficit. Stabilizing the debt needs about 2.9% of GDP of adjustment or 5.5% real growth.
Governance: a cash UHI of $30k per adult is 24% of GDP. Financed by borrowing, it pushes debt past 200% of GDP within 5 years.
Business: firm power and grid connections are the scarce asset. AI gains land in profit margins, and the labor share is at a record low 52.8%.
Wage earners and UHI recipients: income stays in dollars through at least 2030.
The real gap is ownership. The bottom half of US households own 0.6% of stocks.

terms.d: Gross domestic product: the total value of everything a country produces in a year. Debts and programs are often measured as a share of it.
Universal high income: a regular payment to every adult, bigger than a basic income, often linked to robots and AI.
The part of national income paid out as wages. The rest goes to owners as profits, rent and interest.
How much the economy grows after removing the effect of rising prices.
Electricity that is available all the time, not only when the sun shines or the wind blows.

views.why: It helps you see which seat you sit in. If your income is wages or a government check, power prices and ownership matter more to you than the latest crypto news.

connects.how: The tiers section zooms in on the third seat: owners versus people who live on an income stream.
The governance view rests on the debt arithmetic in the debt section.
Round 2 gives these same three views for every answer it publishes.

check.q: According to the desk, what is the real gap for wage earners and UHI recipients?
check.a: Ownership. The bottom half of US households own only 0.6% of stocks, and asset values follow the capital share while wages do not.

tiers.title: Owners and everyone else
tiers.oneLine: The three tiers (asset owners, UHI recipients, workers) behave like two classes: people who own assets and people who live on an income stream.
tiers.picture: Imagine an escalator and a staircase side by side. The owner stands on the escalator, and their assets climb by themselves. The worker and the UHI recipient walk the stairs, rising only as fast as their pay or check rises. Everyone moves up, but the gap keeps growing.
steps: UHI recipients do not lose credit under current law. Lenders may not discriminate against public assistance income (ECOA), and Fannie Mae counts it if it will continue 3 years.
What creates an underclass is access to ownership. The top 10% hold 88.1% of US stocks and funds, the bottom half 0.6%.
A $2,500 a month income supports about a $178k mortgage, while asset prices compound with the capital share.
One possible fix is paying part of a UHI as ownership. Live examples: Trump Accounts (about 70M children, $1,000 seed) and the Alaska Permanent Fund.
Workers are paid in cash by law. For tasks robots can do, wages drift toward the robot's hourly cost, about $2 to $10.

terms.d: Something you own that has value and may grow or pay you, like shares, a home or a business.
Someone who lives on a flow of payments, such as wages or a government check, rather than on what they own.
The part of national income that goes to owners of businesses and property, the mirror of the labor share.
The Equal Credit Opportunity Act, a US law that bans lenders from discriminating, including against people on public assistance.
A US savings account for children with a $1,000 government seed for births from 2025 to 2028, locked until age 18.

tiers.why: It reframes the 'permanent underclass' fear. The danger is less about being refused a loan and more about never owning anything that grows. Owning even a small slice changes which side of the line you stand on.

connects.how: Round 2 asks whether an 18-year-old can still climb from wages to ownership.
Round 2 tests whether a UHI can be used to borrow, and what it really buys.
The wage earner seat in the views section is the same group seen from another angle.

check.q: Do UHI recipients lose access to credit under current US law?
check.a: No. Lenders may not discriminate against public assistance income, and Fannie Mae counts it if it continues at least 3 years. The bigger issue is access to ownership.

r2-lead.title: New rails, old anchors
r2-lead.oneLine: Money is getting new plumbing (stablecoins, tokens, AI agents paying), but the assets underneath stay the same, and ownership decides who keeps up.
r2-lead.picture: Think of an old house getting smart pipes and an app-controlled tap. The water still comes from the same reservoir. Stablecoins and tokens are the smart pipes, and Treasury bills, gold and bank credit are the reservoir.
steps: New rails: every compliant stablecoin must hold Treasury bills of 93 days or less, so new plumbing means more demand for old bonds.
Gold stays the reserve that states buy when they fear sanctions. Central banks bought 863t in 2025.
A UHI check is worth what it buys: real = nominal / (1 + inflation). A digital token changes delivery, not buying power.
Ownership is the dividing line. Since 2019 Q4 the top 10% took 67.5% of the $78.1T rise in US household wealth, the bottom half 3.1%.
For an 18-year-old, the housing rung broke, and a cheap but crowded business launch rung appeared.
Rivals' strongest card is hardware (magnets, batteries, solar wafers), not currency. The next hard date is 10 November 2026.

terms.d: The systems money travels on, such as card networks, bank transfers or blockchains.
The asset that gives money its trust and value underneath, such as Treasury bills or gold.
The number written on a check or price tag, before adjusting for inflation.
What money actually buys after adjusting for price changes.
Everything families own (homes, stocks, savings) minus what they owe.

r2-lead.why: It gives one picture for all ten questions. Whatever new app your money arrives in, two questions stay useful: what sits underneath it, and do you own anything that grows?

connects.how: The Set 1 group explains the old anchors in detail.
The UHI group works through the real versus nominal math.
The entry group shows the broken housing rung and the new launch rung.

check.q: In the 'new rails, old anchors' picture, what are the rails and what are the anchors?
check.a: The rails are the new plumbing: stablecoins, tokens and AI agent payments. The anchors are the old assets: Treasury bills, gold and regulated bank credit.

r2-set1.title: Does the old layer survive?
r2-set1.oneLine: Gold, bonds and bank credit are not disappearing, the new token rails are being built on top of them, by law.
r2-set1.picture: Picture a big oil tanker that used to carry Gulf oil money back to buy US bonds. Now a swarm of small delivery drones does the same trip: foreign savers buy dollar stablecoins, and by law the issuers buy short Treasury bills. The cargo still ends up in the same warehouse.
steps: Set 1 does three jobs: gold is a neutral reserve with no issuer, Treasuries are the prime collateral, and banks create most credit.
From 2027-01-18 compliant stablecoins must hold cash, deposits or bills of 93 days or less. Each new stablecoin dollar is new demand for bonds.
The old petrodollar loop is already small. Saudi Arabia holds $141.2B of Treasuries, 1.5% of foreign holdings.
Stablecoins take over the recycling job, and Gulf money also buys US data centers as owners.
Banks move upstream: their loans to nonbank lenders rose 19.9% in a year to $2.06T.
Borrowing against your future income still needs a regulated lender. DeFi only lends against what you already own.

terms.d: Oil exporters earning dollars and lending them back to the US by buying Treasury bonds.
The US stablecoin law. It requires safe reserves and bans issuers from paying holders interest.
A company that makes loans but does not take deposits, often funded by banks behind the scenes.
Decentralized finance: lending and trading run by software on blockchains, with no bank in the middle.
How much you can borrow compared with what your collateral is worth. 73% means $73 per $100 pledged.

r2-set1.why: In the desk's one-year model, $50,000 at the 0.38% average savings rate earns about $190, while a T-bill fund at about 4.25% earns about $2,125. New rails attack that gap. Loans, though, still come from a lender who checks your income.

connects.how: Round 1's board found the old system buying the new rails. This group checks it in depth.
Stablecoins forced into bills are part of the captive-demand plan for the debt.
If a UHI were paid as an idle stablecoin, the float would go to issuers, not to you.

check.q: Can a stablecoin lend you money for a mortgage?
check.a: No. Stablecoins cannot lend at all, and DeFi lends only against what you already own. A mortgage needs a lender who checks your future income, which stays with banks and bank-funded lenders through at least 2035.

r2-uhi.title: What a basic income check really buys
r2-uhi.oneLine: A UHI check is worth what it buys, so how it is funded decides its real value, and the law decides whether you can borrow against it.
r2-uhi.picture: Imagine getting the same $1,000 banknote every month, while the shopping basket it fills gets a little smaller each time. In a strong-currency country the basket barely shrinks. In a weak-currency country that prints the money, it shrinks fast, especially the imported items like fuel and phones.
steps: Nominal is the number on the check, real is what it buys: real = nominal / (1 + inflation).
Funded from taxes or a fund, prices stay calm. Hong Kong paid 2.7% of GDP in 2020 and inflation was 0.3%.
Printed in a weak currency, the check erodes. Iran's fixed transfer lost about 58% of its real value in five years.
Toy model: a printed UHI worth 10% of GDP keeps about 96% of its value in a US-like economy, but about 78% in local goods and 64% in imports in an Argentina-like one.
You can borrow against a UHI as income, about $69k of mortgage per $1,000 a month. Selling the stream is banned for Social Security, and buyers have paid 30 to 60 cents on the dollar.
A digital token changes delivery, programming and pledging, not the budget limit.

terms.d: The general rise in prices over time, which makes each unit of money buy less.
Automatically raised in line with prices, so the payment keeps its buying power.
To promise an asset or income to a lender as security for a loan.
The US advantage that foreigners want to hold dollars, so it can create some money without much inflation. It is real but limited.
A law (42 USC 407 for Social Security) that bans selling or signing away future benefit payments.

r2-uhi.why: Any promise of a monthly check should be judged by what it buys after a year, not by its headline number. And offers to buy future payments for a lump sum have historically cost 100% or more a year.

connects.how: The UHI table shows nominal versus real values country by country.
Round 1's tiers section first found that UHI income counts for credit.
A UHI paid as a stablecoin would earn its holder nothing, by the same law.

check.q: A $1,000 check arrives after prices rose 25% in a year. Roughly what is it worth in last year's money?

r2-entry.title: Is the ladder still there at 18?
r2-entry.oneLine: The route from first job to owning assets still exists, but the housing rung broke and the business launch rung got cheap but crowded.
r2-entry.picture: Picture a ladder up the side of a building. The bottom rungs, a first job and a credit file, are still there. The middle rung, buying a first home, has cracked. Next to it someone bolted a cheap rope ladder, launching an online brand: easy to grab, but steep and crowded, and only a few reach the top.
steps: First job: unemployment for ages 20 to 24 was 8.0% in September 2026, down from 9.2% a year earlier. AI-exposed entry roles are thinning.
Credit file: a speed bump, not a wall. Authorized-user status, a secured card or a credit-builder loan can start one.
Housing: a 10% down payment for a 20 to 24-year-old saving 10% of pay took about 6.2 years in 1990 and about 10.0 years now (model). The median first-time buyer is a record 40 years old.
Launch: a digital brand costs about $525 to $2,850, but median solo-founder revenue fell 23% in 2025 while the top tenth rose 19%.
Family money is the real seed round: 47% of 18 to 29-year-olds got outside help.
The gap becomes permanent only if asset returns beat wages, housing stays blocked and ownership grants stay tiny into H1.

terms.d: The cash you pay upfront when buying a home. The loan covers the rest.
Your record of borrowing and repaying, which lenders check before giving you credit.
A credit card backed by a cash deposit you put down. It helps build a credit file safely.
The first money put into a new business, often from founders, family or early investors.
Working in a job that does not need your level of training, such as a graduate in a non-graduate job.

r2-entry.why: If you are young, or raising someone who is, this shows where the ladder is weak. The data say ownership, not credit, decides who keeps up, and the housing gate is the down payment, not the monthly bill.

connects.how: Round 1 found that ownership, not credit, is what splits the classes.
The down payment and Trump Account tables put numbers on each rung.
The founders group shows why the cheap launch rung still costs a lot to stay on.

check.q: Which rung does the desk call broken, and why?
check.a: The housing rung. A young earner now needs about 10 years to save a 10% down payment instead of about 6, and the median first-time buyer is a record 40.

r2-founders.title: Cheap to make, costly to sell
r2-founders.oneLine: Robots and cheap energy shrink the part of a product's price that was already small, while shelf space, platforms and ads keep their cut.
r2-founders.picture: Take a $10 lipstick and slice its price like a pizza. The slice the factory and ship touch is small, about $1.76. The store takes about $4.00, ads about $1.47, and the brand's people and warehouses about $2.30. Robots can only nibble at the small slice.
steps: Making and shipping a $10 mass cosmetic costs about $1.76: materials, packaging, labor, inbound freight and duty.
The retailer keeps about $4.00, marketing takes about $1.47, other overhead about $2.30, and profit is about $0.27 (model on e.l.f.'s filings).
A strong robot and energy shock saves maybe 36 cents. Tariffs moved e.l.f.'s margin by a similar amount in one year.
Packaged food is different. At General Mills, cost of sales is 66.4%, so robots and freight matter most on the grocery shelf.
Ocean freight is about 2 cents per lipstick. The last mile costs dollars, about $4.86 as an average fulfillment fee.
Seasonal swings (Q4, Lunar New Year) stay, because they come from demand and capacity, not fuel.

terms.d: What it costs to make the product: materials, factory labor, packaging and getting it to the warehouse.
The share of the shelf price the store keeps.
The share of each sale an online marketplace keeps in fees and ads. Amazon takes 50 to 60% for a typical seller.
The final delivery step, from a local warehouse to your door. It is the most expensive part of shipping.
A product sold under the retailer's own name. Store brands hit a record 24% unit share in H1 2026.

r2-founders.why: It explains why groceries and store brands may get cheaper before branded makeup does. For anyone dreaming of starting a brand, the hard cost is being seen, not making the product.

connects.how: The $10 cost stack table shows each slice and what robots can cut.
This is why the cheap launch rung is crowded: launching is cheap, getting noticed is not.
Electric trucks cut fuel risk but add battery risk, much of it tied to China.

check.q: Of a $10 lipstick's price, roughly how much goes to making and shipping it, and how much to the retailer?
check.a: About $1.76 to making and shipping it, and about $4.00 to the retailer. That is why robots alone cannot make branded goods much cheaper.

r2-rivals.title: Rivals' real lever, and the 'In Time' fear
r2-rivals.oneLine: Rivals' strongest card against the US is energy hardware, not currency, and the 'In Time' fear is half right: goods got cheaper in hours of work, while entry assets got dearer.
r2-rivals.picture: Imagine a town where the bank prints the money, but one neighbor owns the only factory making light bulbs and batteries. The bank can print all it likes. If the neighbor stops selling bulbs, the lights still go out. Treasury can issue bills, but it cannot issue a magnet.
steps: Money moves have little bite. China still holds $590.7B of Treasuries, mBridge has done about $55B in total, and BRICS agreed on no currency.

Hardware moves are live: rare-earth licensing since April 2025, and proposed bans on exporting 12 solar technologies from 16 October 2026. China holds above 94% of polysilicon and 97% of wafer capacity.
The next hard date is 10 November 2026, when China's rare-earth truce lapses or is renewed.
Measured in hours of work since 1990, food at home is 24% cheaper and quality-adjusted cars 54% cheaper.
But the monthly payment on a median home went from about 40 to about 68 hours of work since early 2020.
Owning even a small slice of assets is what stops the clock. The top 10% took 67.5% of the $78.1T wealth rise since 2019 Q4.

terms.d: A group of metals used in strong magnets for motors, wind turbines and electronics. China dominates their processing.
A government rule that limits what can be sold or shared abroad.
A shared digital platform for central banks to settle cross-border payments without the dollar.
A group of countries including Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa that meets on trade and finance.
The hours of work needed to buy something. It shows real affordability better than price tags do.
The idea that people closest to new money, often owners, gain first, before prices adjust for everyone else.

r2-rivals.why: A squeeze from rivals would likely show up as higher power bills and pricier electric cars and home batteries, not as a dollar crash. Measuring prices in hours of your own work shows where life got easier (goods) and harder (homes, health cover).

connects.how: Hardware controls target the watt-dollar described in the core answer.
The time prices and rival levers tables hold the numbers behind this group.
The 'In Time' squeeze lands hardest on the broken housing rung.

check.q: Why does the desk rank China's magnet controls far above a BRICS currency as a threat?
check.a: Because the US can issue dollars but not magnets. Hardware controls hit the energy build-out directly, while a BRICS currency was not even agreed (threat score 3.20 against 0.12).

r2-tables.title: The Round 2 numbers
r2-tables.oneLine: Seven tables turn the Round 2 answers into numbers you can check: real UHI value, a $10 cost stack, a Trump Account at 18, down payment years, time prices, rival levers and Round 3 questions.
r2-tables.picture: Think of the nutrition label on a cereal box. The front says 'healthy', and the label tells you the grams. These tables are the nutrition labels behind the Round 2 answers.
steps: UHI table: of a printed UHI worth 10.00, 9.58 of buying power survives in local goods in a US-like case, and 7.81 in an Argentina-like case.
Cost stack: of a $10 cosmetic, product cost is $1.76 and the retailer margin $4.00.
Trump Account: the $1,000 seed alone is about $2,366 at 18 (5% real). Seed plus $100 a month is about $36,556.
Down payment: 10% down at a 10% savings rate took a young earner 6.2 years in 1990 and 10.0 years in 2026.
Time prices: hours of work for food at home fell 24% since 1990, while a family health premium rose 101% since 1999.
Rival levers and Round 3: threats ranked by score, and twelve open questions that would most change the answers.

terms.d: Arithmetic on stated inputs, not measured data. It shows what follows if the assumptions hold.
Investment growth after subtracting inflation.
Earning returns on past returns, so money grows faster the longer it stays invested.
A future amount shrunk back to what it would buy now, so it can be compared fairly.
The desk's judgment score: cost to the US times likelihood times (6 minus cost to the rival), divided by 25.

r2-tables.why: Numbers make claims testable. You can compare your own situation, such as how many years of saving a home would take, and see whether the story holds for you.

connects.how: The UHI table backs the nominal versus real answers in the UHI group.
The Trump Account and down payment tables back the entry group.
The $10 cost stack backs the founders group.

check.q: In the Trump Account table, what decides most of the value at 18: the $1,000 seed or family contributions?
check.a: Family contributions. The seed alone grows to about $2,366 in today's dollars at 5% real, while adding $100 a month reaches about $36,556.

audit.title: Fact-checking the thesis
audit.oneLine: The desk tested each claim in the owner's newsletter against data and rewrote the ones that failed.
audit.picture: Think of a friend who reads your essay before you hand it in. They do not just cross things out, they show you the right number and suggest a better sentence. That is what this audit does, claim by claim.
steps: Take one claim, for example 'gold times 10 leverage equals world debt'.
Find the real numbers. Gold is worth $29.6T and world debt about $365T, so about 12 times. That ratio wandered from 35 times (1971) to 53 times (2000), so it is a coincidence, not a mechanism.
Give a verdict: confirmed, refuted, misattributed or outdated.
Write the fix: 'Since 1971 nothing physical caps credit. The collateral that anchors the system is US Treasuries.'
Keep what survives: interest on US debt really does exceed military spending, confirmed for FY2024, FY2025 and FY2026.

terms.d: The old textbook idea that banks lend out a fixed multiple of their reserves. The Bank of England says loans create deposits with no fixed multiplier.
Using borrowed money to control more than you own. Ten times leverage means $10 of exposure for each $1 of your own.
A real quote or idea credited to the wrong person.
Cash plus the money people keep in bank accounts. World broad money is about $19.5k per person now.
A loan backed by collateral worth more than the loan itself, as is common in crypto lending.

audit.why: Viral money claims spread fast, and many have the wrong number or the wrong source. Watching one get checked teaches you three questions: what is the real number, who actually said it, and when.

connects.how: The method section explains the seven moves used to check each claim.
Every number in the audit can be traced in the claims ledger.
Some audit verdicts, like the Bessent case, come from debate court cards.

check.q: Do banks multiply money by a fixed factor of 10, as the newsletter claimed?
check.a: No. The Bank of England's 2014 paper says loans create deposits with no fixed multiplier, so the desk marked that line refuted.

method.title: How the desk thinks
method.oneLine: The desk follows seven moves and ranks every piece of evidence by how hard it is to fake.
method.picture: Think of a detective who notices the butler's shoes are clean on a muddy night. Instead of just asking the butler, the detective checks where the money went and when. The desk did that with the Bessent story: it spotted the oddity, then checked Treasury's own fund statement.
steps: Spot the anomaly. In the test case, the US sold euros, not dollars.
State the default move, then map every actor's incentives.
Read the actor's own history and build the chain of cause and effect.
Name tests you can observe and check them: $500M on Treasury's fund statement, against Japan's roughly $97B.
Separate fact from inference, and rank evidence from T0 (money moved) down to T5 (commentary).
When tiers conflict, the higher one wins. A thesis is Confirmed only with T0 or T1 support.

terms.d: Something that does not fit the usual pattern. It is often the best clue to what is really going on.
What a person or institution gains or loses from an action. It helps predict what they will actually do.
The step-by-step path from a cause to an effect, each step something you could check.
A ranking of evidence strength, from T0 (money actually moved) to T5 (commentary without data).
A conclusion reasoned from facts, not a fact itself.
Running the method on a case where an expert answer already exists, to see if the method matches or beats it.

method.why: Much money news is opinion dressed as fact. If you learn to ask 'did money actually move, or did someone just say it?', you can sort headlines in seconds.

connects.how: Every claim in the ledger carries one of these T0 to T5 tiers.
The audit applies this method to the owner's newsletter claims.
Each thesis card's status depends on the tiers of evidence behind it.

check.q: Which evidence wins: an official's speech (T2) or a recorded money flow (T0)?
check.a: The money flow. T0 means money actually moved, and when tiers conflict the higher one wins.

watch.title: Tripwires to watch
watch.oneLine: A short list of dates and numbers that would tell us which future is winning.
watch.picture: Think of the warning lights on a car dashboard. Most of the time they stay dark. When one lights up, oil pressure or engine heat, you know exactly which problem is building. Each tripwire here is one of those lights.
steps: Each indicator has a value now and a tripwire level.
Net interest is 19.5% of federal receipts. At 25% it signals fiscal dominance.
Stablecoins are 4.3% of T-bills. At 10% the dollar extension scenario gets a real funding channel.
The yen is near 158 per dollar. The 160 to 164 zone is where Japan tends to step in.
Dated events: FOMC on 2026-10-28, Treasury refunding on 2026-11-04, the stablecoin law switching on 2027-01-18, and the CBDC ban expiring 2030-12-31.

terms.d: A preset level or event that, if reached, tells you the situation has changed.
The Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed group that sets the main US interest rate.
Treasury's regular announcement of how much debt it will sell, and in what lengths.
A bond's interest rate minus expected inflation: what lenders really earn.
The gap between two interest rates, such as France's versus Germany's. A widening spread signals rising worry.

watch.why: You do not need to follow markets every day. A handful of signals, checked now and then, tells you whether the big picture is shifting. It also guards against panic when a scary headline hits but no tripwire has moved.

connects.how: Each tripwire is tied to a scenario it would strengthen.
Watching these signals is how the bands on the future map would get redrawn.
Several tripwires, like net interest and real yields, track the debt treadmill.

check.q: Stablecoins are 4.3% of T-bills today. What level would make them a real funding channel for the dollar?
check.a: 10% of T-bills, the tripwire the desk set for the dollar extension scenario.

cards.title: Thesis cards from the debate court
cards.oneLine: Each card is one claim that went through a six-role debate, with a status and the judge's confidence that it is true.
cards.picture: Imagine a courtroom where each claim is on trial. One lawyer argues for it, one against, an accountant checks the math, a historian checks the past, someone asks who profits, and a judge gives a verdict and a percentage. Each card is that verdict, written on an index card.
steps: A claim goes before a panel: proponent, skeptic, accountant, historian, incentive mapper and judge.
The judge gives a status: confirmed, plausible, speculative or refuted.
The judge also gives a confidence number. Example: 'Net interest exceeds defense spending' is confirmed at 95.
Each card has a horizon, H0 to H3, for when it applies.
Cards sit in clusters (energy, strategy, debt, tiers), and you can filter by cluster or status.

terms.d: A clear claim that can be tested and proven right or wrong.
The debater who makes the strongest case for the claim.
The debater who makes the strongest case against the claim.
The judge's estimate, from 0 to 100, of how likely the statement is to be true.
The verdict word: confirmed (backed by hard evidence), plausible (likely but not proven), speculative (possible, thin evidence) or refuted (shown false).

cards.why: Instead of one opinion, you see how strong each claim is. A 'plausible 60' is a lean, not a fact, and knowing the difference keeps you from overreacting.

connects.how: Each card points back to claims in the ledger that support or weaken it.
The evidence tiers decide whether a card can be marked confirmed.
The core answer rests on card Da-08, plausible at 65.

check.q: What does a card marked 'plausible 60' tell you?
check.a: The panel found the claim reasonable but not proven, and the judge puts the chance it is true at about 60 in 100.

evidence.title: Raw sources and the claims ledger
evidence.oneLine: Every claim the desk uses sits in a searchable ledger with its evidence tier, status, source and date, so you can check anything yourself.
evidence.picture: Think of the receipts drawer in a kitchen. The note on the fridge says 'we spent $400 on food this month'. If you doubt it, you open the drawer and find every receipt with its date. The ledger is that drawer for this research.
steps: Each claim gets an ID (for example L1-01), the claim itself, a source link and dates.
It gets an evidence tier: T0 money moved, T1 law, T2 officials on record, T3 market prices, T4 specialist analysis, T5 commentary.
It gets a status (confirmed, plausible, speculative or refuted) and a falsifier: what would prove it wrong.
The ledger holds 419 claims from the research tracks, the reloop and Round 2.
Search by word, filter by status or track, and follow the source link.

terms.d: A running list of records. Here, every claim with its source and rating.
How strong the evidence is, from T0 (money actually moved) to T5 (commentary without data).
The specific fact or event that would show a claim is wrong. Good claims always name one.
The date the claim was last checked as true. Money facts go stale fast.
The original document, such as a law, a filing or an official data release, rather than a report about it.

evidence.why: Trust should be checkable. When a page says something about your money, you should be able to see where the number came from and how old it is.

connects.how: The method section explains the tiers used to rate each claim.
The thesis cards are built from claims in this ledger.
The audit verdicts can be traced to their claims here.

check.q: A claim comes from an analyst's report, and nobody has seen money move. Which tier is it?
check.a: T4, specialist analysis. It ranks below market prices (T3), officials on record (T2), law (T1) and money actually moving (T0).
